title: Rama in every tree
hookLine: an old rakshasa admits that he sees Rama behind every tree in the forest
carry: smarana: remembering god, even through fear

cards: Maricha has given his king the argument. Now he gives him something more personal: his fear. Let me tell you how I know Rama, he says.
I was strong once, and proud. I went to break up Vishvamitra's sacrifice, and a boy, barely grown, shot me with one arrow and threw me a hundred yojanas into the sea. I lived.
And I didn't learn, not then. It took a second meeting.

teach.h: I SEE RAMA IN EVERY TREE.
teach.b: Later, Maricha says, I came into Dandaka with two others, all three of us in the shape of deer, eating sages. Rama saw us and shot three arrows. My two companions died.
I ran. Since then I've given all that up. But I can't get away from him.
I see Rama in every tree, dressed in bark, holding his bow. I see him in my dreams. Even words that start with his sound, ratna, jewel, ratha, chariot, frighten me.
Then Ravana answers. I didn't come for advice.

teach.h: OBEY, OR I KILL YOU NOW.
teach.b: Do as I say, or I'll kill you now. Maricha sees the trap: Rama kills me if I go, you kill me if I don't. Better to die at the hands of an enemy like Rama, he says.
And he goes. Now look again at that confession, because Hindu teachers have. Maricha can't stop thinking of Rama.

teach.h: LOVE, FEAR OR HATRED: THE MIND ON GOD.
teach.b: The Bhagavata Purana says something startling about minds like that: the gopis fixed their minds on Krishna through love, King Kamsa through fear, others through hatred, and all of them came to him, because their minds were full of God.
Remembering God has a name, smarana, and it's one of the classic forms of bhakti. Maricha does it by accident, out of fear.

teach.h: BETTER TO DIE BY RAMA'S HAND.
teach.b: Devotees do it on purpose, out of love: saying Rama's name through the day, writing Shri Ram line after line in a notebook. In Tulsidas's telling, Maricha even goes gladly, thinking at least he'll see Rama before he dies.
And the week behind us: a proposal and a wound, an army and a promise kept, a king's pride, and an old enemy who couldn't stop seeing Rama.

how: Some Ramayana teachers set Maricha's confession, seeing Rama in every tree, beside the Bhagavata's teaching that a mind fixed on God, even through fear, comes to him; devotees practice smarana on purpose, through the name and Ram naam lekhan, writing Rama's name.

o: the rakshasa who sees Rama in every tree, and goes anyway
the rakshasa who first suggests carrying off Sita
a sage whose sacrifice Rama guarded as a boy

p: a hundred yojanas into the sea
obey, or I kill you now
remembering God, a form of bhakti

s: in Hindu teaching, only loving thoughts of God count
the Bhagavata says Kamsa came to God through fear and the gopis through love: the mind fixed on God is what matters.
Maricha tells Ravana he has met Rama twice before
at Vishvamitra's sacrifice, and later in Dandaka as a deer.
Maricha agrees because he believes the plan will work
he agrees because he'd rather die by Rama's hand than his king's.

games.q: a friend says they only think about God when they're scared, so it 'doesn't count.' by today's teaching, what fits?
o: it counts: a mind turning to God, even in fear, is turning toward him.
it doesn't count; only calm, loving prayer reaches God.
fear means you don't really believe, so drop it.
games.why: Maricha remembered Rama out of fear. the Bhagavata says Kamsa reached God through fear, and the gopis through love, the way devotees choose. smarana is the remembering.

practice: Sit comfortably and let your eyes close. If you pray, let a name of God ride on your breath: Ram, or whichever name is yours, once in, once out. When your mind wanders, and it will, bring it back to the name.
If you don't pray, use a word that steadies you, like peace. Maricha couldn't stop remembering. Here, you choose to.

wordCard.voice: Maricha, the rakshasa who confesses his fear, is threatened by Ravana, and agrees to go: better to die by Rama's hand than by his own king.

orig.note: Sanskrit mārīca: the rakshasa spared at Siddhashrama, who becomes the golden deer.

carryVoice: Keep this: smarana, remembering God, even through fear. Tomorrow, a deer made of gold. Another week, done.
